title: Sound and click latencies of 132-158 mouse brain regions followed Knox input sources beyond distance and cell types, but net projection direction did not predict response order (IBL)
abstract: Question: earlier work found that regions with similar axonal inputs have similar task coding, and regions with a similar cell-type mix have similar intrinsic spiking. A similarity has no direction. Does response timing, which has a direction, follow the mesoscale connectome? Data: IBL Brain-Wide Map passive-replay responses (607 probes, 398 sessions, 65,772 good units) to sounds, valve clicks and Gabor patches; we read only the passive segment of each spike file with HTTP range requests. Structure: Knox 2019 connectome, Allen CCF centroids, Allen MERFISH subclass mix. Method: a plan frozen before any latency was computed; region latency is the half-maximum time of the mean normalised response of responsive units; inference used 1,000 spatial surrogate maps, with post-freeze calibration on synthetic maps. Results: sound (132 regions, median 11.8 ms) and valve-click (158 regions) latency maps were reliable (split-half rho 0.46 and 0.54); the visual map was not (rho 0.07; 2.1% responsive units). The pre-registered direction test failed: the net projection asymmetry of a region pair did not predict which region responded later (sound p = 0.71; visual 0.52; valve 0.87); the raw order was reversed because Knox net flow is mostly corticofugal and brainstem, midbrain and thalamic targets responded first. The pre-registered visual-minus-sound test also failed (p = 0.49) because the visual map was noise. But region latency followed the input-weighted latency of input sources beyond distance, division, co-recording and cell-type mix: full-model beta 0.39 for sound (surrogate p = 0.007) and 0.95 for valve (p = 0.001); no synthetic no-wiring map reached these p values. Cell-type mix did not predict latency (p 0.82-0.89). Input and output wiring predicted latency equally (difference p 0.20-0.25), and division-plus-distance rewired nulls were liberal (31-36% false positives). Conclusion: sensory timing, like task coding, goes with wiring and not with cell types, but these data do not show a source-to-target direction. Limitations: correlational region averages, one connectome model, few passive trials, possible startle or movement responses, surrogate tests 9-12% liberal on synthetic maps, and the positive result rests on secondary and post-freeze analyses.
